title: United States v. Gray (published opinion and companion summary order)
lead: Private-prison officers’ false records concerned a matter within federal jurisdiction even before a federal investigation began, and two appellate writings resolved their remaining challenges.

actors.name: Rex Eguridu
actors.role: Federal inmate involved in the force incident

proceedings: District court jury trial: Wells and Rhodes convicted on specified obstruction and false-statement counts, with separate acquittals.
Second Circuit: published § 1519 opinion and companion summary order affirmed both judgments.
limits: The decision does not make every private investigation federally cognizable. Knowledge-of-federal-jurisdiction arguments had preservation and evidence qualifications. Wells’s force acquittal and others’ conspiracy acquittals remain distinct from affirmed convictions.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An incident involving a federal prisoner leads to false reports
sections.cue: Introduce the institution and the concealment evidence.
paragraphs: Marvin Wells and Stephen Rhodes worked at Queens Private Correctional Facility, which housed federal prisoners under a United States Marshals Service contract. Although Kirby Gray came first in the case caption, Wells and Rhodes were the appellants.

The record described Wells strip-searching inmate Rex Eguridu on April 17, 2007, striking his chest and throat so his head repeatedly hit a concrete wall, and threatening him against reporting. Rhodes and Gray witnessed the encounter. Inaccurate reports and efforts to make other officers repeat a false account followed. Officer Andrews supplied a truthful version in her fifth report, and Officer Day in his second. Private operation later became important to the officers’ argument that an internal investigation fell outside federal obstruction law.

Department of Justice Inspector General agents interviewed officers in 2008, and Wells and Rhodes made false statements. A November 12 indictment led to a jury trial before District Judge Jack B. Weinstein.

sections.title: The verdict separates obstruction from the force charge
sections.cue: State the convictions, sentences, and coordinated appellate review.
paragraphs: The April 1, 2010 judgments convicted Wells of conspiracy under 18 U.S.C. § 371, record obstruction under § 1519, two attempted-intimidation and corrupt-persuasion counts under § 1512(b)(3), and a false statement under § 1001(a)(2). Rhodes was convicted under §§ 1519 and 1001(a)(2). Wells received a year and a day in prison and three years’ supervised release; Rhodes received three years’ probation.
The jury acquitted Wells of excessive force and acquitted Rhodes and Gray of conspiracy. Those acquittals did not erase the other verdicts.

On April 28, 2011, Judge Robert A. Katzmann wrote a published opinion on § 1519, while an unsigned companion order addressed the remaining arguments. Judges Kearse, Sack, and Katzmann formed the unanimous panel, with no separate writing.

sections.title: Section 1519 does not import another statute’s official-proceeding nexus
sections.cue: Follow the textual distinction and its application.
paragraphs: Wells and Rhodes argued that falsification needed a nexus to a pending or imminent official proceeding. Aguilar interpreted § 1503’s administration-of-justice language, and Arthur Andersen interpreted § 1512(b)(2), which expressly mentioned an official proceeding. Section 1519 instead covered knowing falsification, concealment, or destruction with intent to obstruct investigation or proper administration of a matter within an agency’s jurisdiction, including acts in contemplation of it.

The panel refused to import wording from those other offenses. No proceeding or investigation had to be underway or about to begin. Senate history reinforced a design to avoid technical pending-proceeding limitations; it supported rather than replaced the textual distinction. Contrary language in Russell about a particular anticipated federal investigation was not followed.

The underlying force matter fell within Justice Department authority because this prison performed federal custody functions under contract and had force-reporting duties. Initial internal review did not privatize a matter involving federal prisoners. Eventual federal investigation confirmed the practical relationship but was not a prerequisite at falsification.

The officers’ lack of knowledge that reports would reach federal investigators did not establish a requirement of awareness of a pending investigation. Their broader objection about knowing federal jurisdiction was unpreserved against the instruction, and training and institutional duties supplied ample awareness evidence anyway. Those grounds did not settle a universal knowledge-of-jurisdiction rule. Knowing falsification and obstructive intent still applied, and other private investigations were expressly reserved.

sections.title: The companion order sustains witness-pressure and false-statement convictions
sections.cue: Explain the other statutory elements separately.
paragraphs: For Wells’s § 1512(b)(3) counts, the companion order explained that protection covered communications about possible federal offenses and potential witnesses. No proceeding had to be pending or imminent under § 1512(f)(1), and § 1512(g) did not require knowing an officer’s federal identity. Initial communications inside the prison could therefore qualify. Justice Department policy on force against federal prisoners and the evidence, viewed favorably to the government, supported a rational jury’s findings.

Wells also argued Inspector General Agent Mary Chiu-Vaccariello had not relied on his statements. Materiality required a natural tendency or capacity to affect decision-making, not actual reliance. His denial of an officer cover-up addressed the investigation’s central subject and could be materially false.

sections.title: Acquittals and policy evidence do not undermine the supported convictions
sections.cue: Close with the evidence review and exact affirmance.
paragraphs: A conspiracy conviction did not automatically fail because alleged coconspirators were acquitted, and inconsistent counts or codefendant verdicts did not by themselves establish insufficient evidence. Applying Powell, the Supreme Court’s inconsistent-verdict precedent, the panel refused to speculate about lenity or jury reasons. Independently reviewed evidence supported Rhodes’s obstruction and false-statement convictions.

The officers also objected that facility force policies were stricter than Bureau of Prisons standards and might mislead jurors. Under abuse-of-discretion review requiring impact on a substantial right, Wells’s acquittal on the force charge undercut that claimed prejudice. The court found no evidentiary abuse.

Together, the published opinion and companion order affirmed both district judgments. They sustained proven concealment under the institution’s particular federal relationship without adjudicating every internal inquiry at every private entity.
